title: Three letters of context
objectives: Build a dataset of three-letter contexts and next letters from a list of names.

screens.title: After em
screens.prose: After em, the bigram model sees only the m. The bars compare what follows m anywhere in the names with what follows the two letters em.
screens.question: Which letter most often follows em?

options.why: a leads after m alone, 2,590 of 6,642. After em, i leads: 160 of 769.
The end follows em 128 times, third after i and a.
m follows em 100 times, as in emma: fourth.

hints.text: Read the bars for em, not those for m.

feedback.correct: i: 160 of 769, though a leads after m alone.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the bars for em, not for m.

byKey.a: You read the bigram row for m. One more letter of context changes the leader to i.

explain.text: After m alone, a leads with a share of 0.39. After em, i leads with 0.21 and a drops to 0.18 (emily, emilia). Two letters of context tell a model more than one.

screens.title: Rows of a dataset
screens.prose: A model that sees three symbols needs rows of (context, next symbol). Pad each name with three start marks: `...emma.`. Slide through the rows.
screens.question: How many rows does emma give?

hints.text: One row per letter, plus one for the end mark.
e, m, m, a and the end: 5 rows.

feedback.correct: 5 rows: one for each letter and one for the end mark.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the symbols that get predicted.

byKey.no-end: You left out the row whose target is the end mark. The model must learn to stop.
byKey.no-pad: You kept only rows with three real letters before them. Padding gives the first letters rows too.

explain.text: Each of e, m, m, a and the end mark is predicted once from the three symbols before it, so emma gives 5 rows. Padding lets the first letter have a context too.

screens.title: X and Y
screens.prose: Name the result: a **dataset** of inputs $X$, each row the **context** of three symbol indices, and targets $Y$, the index that came next. A **block size** of 3 means three symbols of context.

screens.title: How many rows
screens.prose: The 25,626 training names hold 156,905 letters between them.

state.caption: emma as five rows; `.` is 0, a is 1, e is 5, m is 13.

screens.question: How many rows does the training set have?

hints.text: Each name of $L$ letters gives $L + 1$ rows.

feedback.correct: 182,531: one row per letter plus one per name.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each name adds one row for its end mark.

byKey.no-end: You counted one row per letter. Each name also predicts its end mark.
byKey.pads: You counted the symbols of `...emma`, the pads and the letters, $L + 3$ a name. The pads are context only, never targets.

explain.text: Each name of $L$ letters gives $L + 1$ rows, so the training names give $156{,}905 + 25{,}626 = 182{,}531$. The dev and test names give 22,807 and 22,808, the same counts as their bigram pairs.

screens.title: Why not count contexts?
screens.prose: Why not count, as in level 1? A table over three-symbol contexts has one row per context: $27^3 = 19{,}683$ rows of 27 cells. The training rows hold only 5,440 different contexts.
screens.question: What share of the table’s rows would never be seen in training? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.correct: $14{,}243 / 19{,}683 = 0.72$: most rows would be pure smoothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the unseen contexts by all of them.

byKey.seen: That is the share seen. The question asks for the rows never seen.

explain.text: $14{,}243$ of the $19{,}683$ contexts never occur, a share of 0.72, and many seen ones occur once or twice. A count table cannot share what it learns about em with what it learns about am; a network with embeddings can.

screens.title: Across the boundary
screens.prose: A learner joins all the names into one string, `.emma.olivia.ava.`, and slides a window of three over it.
screens.question: What is wrong with the row `ma.` then o?

options.text: olivia’s first letter is predicted from the end of emma
Nothing: the end mark separates the names
options.why: The mark is in the context, but so are m and a from emma; a new name should start from `...`.
It has three symbols, as asked; the trouble is which three.

hints.text: What context does a name really start from?
Every name starts after nothing: `...`. Here olivia starts after emma.

feedback.correct: Each name must start from `...`; joining them leaks the last name into the next.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the model learns about how names begin.

byKey.fine: You trusted the end mark to reset. The context still holds m and a from emma.

explain.text: Names are independent, so each starts from a context of three marks. Sliding over joined names teaches that olivia’s o depends on emma’s ending, a pattern that is not real. Reset the context at every name.

Every one of the three contexts starts with a mark.

feedback.correct: All 3: `...`, `..j` and `.jo` each hold a start mark.
feedback.generic: Not quite. List the three contexts and look for `.`.

byKey.one: You counted only the all-mark context `...`. `..j` and `.jo` hold marks too.
byKey.two: You counted two; `.jo` still begins with a mark.

explain.text: jo gives 3 rows, `...`, `..j` and `.jo`, and every context holds at least one start mark. A name needs 3 letters before any of its contexts is all letters.

screens.title: Any block size
screens.prose:
The rule for any block size $k$: start each name with $k$ marks, and for every letter and the end mark, record the last $k$ symbols and the symbol itself, then slide.

```python
context = [0] * k
for ch in w + ".":
    X.append(context); Y.append(index[ch])
    context = context[1:] + [index[ch]]
```
screens.question: With $k = 1$, what are the rows?

options.text: Nothing useful: a context needs two symbols
options.why: One symbol of context is exactly what the bigram used.

options.text: One row per letter, with no end rows
options.why: The end mark is still a target, as in the bigram pairs.

hints.text: What does one symbol of context look like?
`.` then e, e then m, ...: the bigram pairs.

feedback.correct: The bigram pairs: block 1 is level 1’s dataset.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Write emma’s rows with a context of one.

explain.text: With $k = 1$ the context is just the previous symbol, so the rows are level 1’s bigram pairs: 182,531 of them on the training names. A bigger $k$ only lengthens each context.

screens.title: Three days of returns
screens.prose: A signal uses the last three daily returns of a share to predict tomorrow’s sign. On the first three days of the series there are not yet three returns before the day.
screens.question: What is the honest way to handle those first days?

options.text: Drop them, or mark the missing returns as missing
Pad with 0: a return of zero
options.why: A return of 0 is a real value, a flat day; the model would learn from days that never happened.

options.text: Take the missing returns from the end of the series
options.why: That uses the future as the past: a look-ahead leak, like joining names.

hints.text: Is a return of 0 the same as no return?
0 is a flat day. A mark that means “nothing yet” is what `.` is for names.

feedback.correct: Drop them or mark them: a pad must mean “no data”, as `.` does for names.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask whether the pad could be mistaken for real data.

byKey.zero: For names, `.` is its own symbol, never a letter. A zero return is a real flat day, so it misleads.

explain.text: The start mark works for names because it is a symbol of its own, never a real letter. A zero return is a real outcome, so padding with it invents flat days. Drop the first days or add an explicit “missing” input.

ideas: After em the names favour i; after m alone, a. More context tells a model more.
Each letter and the end mark is one row: the three symbols before it, padded with `.` at the start of each name. The splits give 182,531, 22,807 and 22,808 rows.
A count table over three-symbol contexts has 19,683 rows and most are never seen, so level 2 uses a network that shares what it learns.
